newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan stands firm against army warning.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan stands firm against army warning.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Tuesday dug in his heels against a military challenge to his rule that has strained the unity of the Islamist-led coalition.
"Parliament gives the job of serving the nation to the government and the government is responsible only to parliament," he told a meeting of his Islam-based Welfare Party.
The military-dominated National Security Council has ordered Erbakan to reverse a recent wave of Islamist zeal partly caused by his Welfare Party in a warning that has shaken the country.

The Hurriyet newspaper said members of pro-Western coalition partner Tansu Ciller's party wanted to split the eight-month-old coalition straight away. But Ciller said she would not abandon the alliance. "No," she said when asked by reporters if she would quit the coalition.

The Milliyet daily had quoted Ciller, a pro-Western conservative who serves as deputy prime minister, as telling her True Path Party on Monday she would desert Erbakan if he did not heed the influential army.

Istanbul stocks plunged more than 12 percent before clawing back to end the day down 5.19 percent, after a drop on Monday of 5.58 percent. Brokers said Tuesday's drop was due to political worries and poor inflation results.
Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, attended last Friday's security meeting but the press says he refused to sign a council statement urging an anti-Islamist crackdown.
"In a way he is challenging the state. He looks like he is rebelling against some of the rules of the democratic system," Anatolian news agency quoted leftist leader Bulent Ecevit as saying.
The National Security Council is legally charged with defending Turkey's official secularism.
Political analysts say he ignores the generals at his peril.
The army, which often leads surveys as the country's most respected institution, has ousted three governments since 1960.

It practically runs nine mainly-Kurdish provinces under emergency rule in the southeast where it has a free hand against separatist rebels. The armed forces play a major role in Turkey's many disputes with neighbours Greece and Cyprus.
Young officers are taught to idolise Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk, himself a military man.
Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, a member of Ciller's wing, predicted the prime minister could quit rather than disappoint his Islamist backers by heeding the army.
Despite the friction, there was no immediate sign that Erbakan would lose two parliamentary challenges on Tuesday.
MPs began debating a motion on whether to go ahead with an opposition censure motion against the coalition within a week.
Deputies will also vote on starting an inquiry into Justice Minister Sevket Kazan, an Islamist and close aide of Erbakan. Defeat on either issue would be a major blow to the government.

If accepted, the inquiry would probe alleged abuse of his position for remarks he made suggesting members of the liberal Alevi Moslem sect take part in incestuous ceremonies and a visit he made to a Welfare mayor jailed for organising an Islamist protest also attended by Iran's ambassador.
